The officials were serving at the consulate in Assosa, the administrative center of Ethiopia's Benishangul-Gumuz region, which borders Sudan. The city lies approximately 476 kilometers (296 miles) west of Addis Ababa and 648 kilometers (403 miles) southeast of Khartoum. Ethiopian authorities have not publicly explained the decision. The move follows complaints by Sudan to the UN Security Council and the African Union's Peace and Security Council accusing Ethiopia of facilitating drone operations by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which has been fighting Sudan's army since April 2023. Sudan's Foreign Ministry said it had submitted documents alleging that drones operating from Ethiopian territory struck civilian areas, electricity facilities and other infrastructure, causing casualties and disrupting essential services. Sudanese presidential adviser Amjad Farid alleged that 70 attacks involving 187 explosive drones were launched from Ethiopia between Feb. 15 and Oct. 27, killing more than 400 civilians. He stressed that Khartoum reserved the right to respond to threats against its sovereignty. Sudan's army-led authorities have also reported hundreds of civilian and military casualties from the strikes. Khartoum has repeatedly accused Addis Ababa of supporting the RSF, though the allegations have not been independently verified. Ethiopia, meanwhile, has accused Sudan of backing armed groups involved in its own internal conflicts. This decision follows Sudan's allegations that drone attacks, reportedly launched from Ethiopian territory, have killed hundreds of civilians. Sudan's Foreign Ministry has accused Ethiopia of facilitating operations by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which has been in conflict with Sudan's army since April 2023. Sudan claims that between February and October 2023, 70 drone attacks originating from Ethiopia resulted in over 400 civilian deaths. In response, Sudan has asserted its right to defend its sovereignty. The diplomatic tensions reflect a broader escalation in relations between the two countries, with each accusing the other of supporting armed groups involved in their respective internal conflicts. Ethiopian authorities have not publicly clarified their reasons for the expulsion of the Sudanese officials.

ethiopia.title: Dakar 2026 - Ethiopian Elsabet Amare Takes Her Racing Dreams from Injibara to Dakar
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia/Senegal: Dakar 2026 - Ethiopian Elsabet Amare Takes Her Racing Dreams from Injibara to Dakar - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia/Senegal: Dakar 2026 - Ethiopian Elsabet Amare Takes Her Racing Dreams from Injibara to Dakar Brook Genene Ruga, Bird Story Agency Elsabet Amare, Ethiopian runner, posing for a photo in October 2026. 4 November 2026 Bird Story Agency (Africa) By Brook Genene Ruga Inspired by her father and Ethiopian distance-running great Meseret Defar, 17-year-old Elsabet Amare is preparing to represent her country at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games. The runner hopes her journey will encourage other young athletes from her hometown of Injibara. Before a race, Ethiopian runner Elsabet Amare tries to stay positive. As she prepares to represent a nation known for its great runners, she hopes the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games will offer another opportunity to win medals. The 17-year-old has already shown what she can do on a big stage. At an under-18 competition in Nigeria in 2025, she waited until the final moments of the 800 metres to make her move. World Athletics described her finish as “a tactical masterclass”. Elsabet sat behind Kenya’s Vicody Chemutai until the final 200 metres, then accelerated to win in 2:02.96. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines “I know I have a strong finishing ability, and that is what I utilised,” she said. Elsabet had won silver in the 1,500 metres at the same competition before lining up for the 800 metres. “I was determined to win Gold in the 800 meter,” she explained. Missing out on gold in the first race motivated her to seize the next opportunity, just as she has done before while pursuing her passion for running. Elsabet grew up in Injibara, a town in the Awi zone of Ethiopia’s Amhara region, about 440 kilometres from Addis Ababa. She credits her father with sparking her interest in the sport. “I started running because of my father. He loved athletics. He used to follow the sport through reading magazines and watching TV,” she said. Her father encouraged her to enter the sport, she said, but never forced her to run. Inspired by him, she began competing at school and represented her school in tournaments. A high school history teacher, her father never taught her in class, but he told her about Ethiopia’s great athletes. “He used to watch the likes of Haile Gebrselassie, Kenenisa Bekele, Tirunesh Dibaba and Meseret Defar,” she said. “I learned about the athletes at school and read about them in our text book.” One athlete in particular captured her attention. “Meseret was the one athlete I used to look up to growing up,” Elsabet said. She admired Defar’s resilience and desire to win and wanted to be like her. Elsabet also speaks of the support young athletes received from their community in Injibara. “Growing up, the community supported all of the young athletes who aspired to make it in the big stages. We had a project where I used to train, and projects like ours used to be supported,” she said. Sport was her favourite subject, and she pursued athletics even though balancing training and schoolwork was difficult. “My teachers used to support me once they knew I had started running. They used to allow me to go to tournaments and helped me to catch up with my schoolwork when I came back,” she explained. Ethiopia’s athletics team has been training for the past six months, she said. “With God’s grace we expect to be successful in Dakar.” As she looks ahead to the Games, Elsabet says the support around her has helped her feel confident. “My coaches always support and motivate me. I am well prepared but not stressed. I will give it my best.” She hopes support for young runners in her home region will continue. “In the region I grew up, there is support, but that needs to continue. There are so many talented runners there.” Just as Meseret Defar inspired her, Elsabet wants her own journey to inspire the athletes who come after her. ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Expels Sudanese Diplomats Amid Regional Tensions | Kulu Media Home Latest News Ethiopia Tigray Eritrea Sudan Africa World Politics Economy Finance Business Education More Analysis Entertainment Tech Health Sports English English ትግርኛ አማርኛ Connect with us Search Kulu Media Ethiopia Orders Six Sudanese Diplomats to Leave as Regional Tensions Escalate Home Latest News Ethiopia Tigray Eritrea Sudan Africa World Politics Economy Finance Business Education More Analysis Entertainment Tech Health Sports English English ትግርኛ አማርኛ Home » News » Ethiopia » Ethiopia Orders Six Sudanese Diplomats to Leave as Regional Tensions Escalate Ethiopia Ethiopia Orders Six Sudanese Diplomats to Leave as Regional Tensions Escalate Six Sudanese consular staff ordered out as Ethiopia-Sudan tensions deepen. Published 6 hours ago on November 4, 2026 By Kulu Media News Desk Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed (left) and Sudanese military leader Abdel Fattah al-Burhan (right), pictured in a composite image as diplomatic tensions between the two countries escalate. Image: Kulu Media (Illustration) Ethiopia has ordered six Sudanese consular staff members to leave the country within 48 hours, deepening a diplomatic dispute between the neighboring countries amid allegations involving Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia. A senior Ethiopian official confirmed the departure order to Reuters in a report published on November 4, 2026. The six officials were stationed at Sudan’s consulate in Assosa, the capital of Ethiopia’s Benishangul-Gumuz region near the Sudanese border. The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, did not explain the reason for the decision. Ethiopia’s government had not publicly provided a detailed explanation of the move at the time of the Reuters report. The expulsion order comes amid worsening relations between Addis Ababa and Khartoum, with both governments accusing each other of involvement in armed conflicts affecting the wider Horn of Africa. Sudan has accused Ethiopia of allowing the RSF to use Ethiopian territory to launch drone attacks against civilian infrastructure inside Sudan. Khartoum says it has submitted complaints to the United Nations Security Council and the African Union’s Peace and Security Council over the alleged attacks. The latest accusations follow months of Ethiopia-Sudan tensions involving border security, drone operations and the wider Sudanese civil war. Sudanese military officials have previously alleged that RSF drones were being launched from Ethiopian territory, claims rejected by Addis Ababa. Ethiopia denies supporting the RSF. The allegations concerning the use of Ethiopian territory for drone operations have not been independently established. The diplomatic dispute has intensified as Sudan’s civil war continues and renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia raises concerns about the security of the region’s shared borders. Ethiopia, meanwhile, has accused neighboring countries of supporting TPLF-aligned forces involved in renewed hostilities against the Ethiopian federal government. The accusations specifically concern Sudan, Eritrea and Egypt, all of which have denied supporting the armed groups. The competing allegations have heightened tensions between governments already facing significant security and diplomatic challenges. Assosa’s location gives the latest development particular significance. The town lies in western Ethiopia, close to Sudan, and serves as an important administrative center in a region affected by cross-border security concerns. Sudan’s consular presence there has provided a channel for official communication and assistance to Sudanese nationals. The departure of the six staff members could further complicate diplomatic engagement, although the immediate consequences for consular services remain unclear. The latest development follows a series of diplomatic confrontations involving Ethiopia and neighboring countries. On October 1, Ethiopia ordered the closure of its embassy in Eritrea and expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats, accusing Asmara of activities threatening Ethiopian national security. Eritrea subsequently announced that it was severing diplomatic relations with Ethiopia, while the two governments exchanged accusations over the renewed conflict in northern Ethiopia. The deterioration in relations coincided with reports of Eritrean military movements inside eastern Tigray and drone strikes reportedly targeting Eritrean forces. The reported incidents further increased concerns about a wider regional confrontation. The diplomatic dispute also extended to Egypt after Addis Ababa ordered an Egyptian diplomat to leave the country and Cairo responded with a reciprocal measure. The African Union called for restraint and urged the governments involved to resolve their differences through diplomatic channels. The growing tensions have renewed concerns that separate conflicts in Ethiopia and Sudan could become increasingly interconnected. Sudan’s civil war began in April 2023 following a power struggle between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the RSF. The conflict has caused widespread destruction, mass displacement and one of the world’s most severe humanitarian emergencies. According to Reuters, more than 14 million people have been displaced by the fighting. The war has also complicated relations with Sudan’s neighbors, particularly as rival parties accuse regional governments of providing military assistance or allowing armed groups to operate across borders. The regional security implications have become increasingly serious as Sudan’s conflict intersects with diplomatic rivalries involving Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt. Military movements near the Ethiopia-Sudan border and competing allegations of foreign support have added to concerns about wider instability. Eritrea has also accused Ethiopia of supporting Sudan’s RSF and destabilizing the Horn of Africa. Addis Ababa has denied supporting the paramilitary group, and the allegations have not been independently verified. In Ethiopia, the renewed confrontation involving federal forces and TPLF-aligned forces has raised fresh concerns about the durability of the November 2022 Pretoria peace agreement, which ended the major phase of the earlier Tigray war. The security situation in northern Ethiopia remains fragile. In October, reported drone strikes near Adigrat were followed by accounts of Eritrean troop movements, illustrating how the renewed conflict has affected relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea. Sudanese presidential adviser Amjad Farid said Khartoum was seeking to avoid an open war with Ethiopia despite the worsening diplomatic situation. Speaking to Reuters, Farid said Sudan remained committed to defending its territory while making efforts to prevent a direct military confrontation. The departure order for the six Sudanese consular staff members adds another layer of uncertainty to relations between Addis Ababa and Khartoum. It remains unclear whether the measure will lead to further diplomatic restrictions, reciprocal expulsions or renewed negotiations between the two governments. With Sudan’s civil war continuing and security tensions rising across northern and western Ethiopia, the latest dispute underscores the risk that unresolved regional disagreements could further undermine stability across the Horn of Africa. Published 8 hours ago on November 4, 2026 By Kulu Media News Desk The US Department of Justice headquarters in Washington, D.C. The department announced that Abraham Teklu Lemma pleaded guilty to transmitting classified intelligence to Ethiopian officials. Credit: APK / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY 4.0 An Ethiopian-born American citizen who previously worked as a US government contractor has pleaded guilty to providing highly classified American intelligence to Ethiopian officials during a period that overlapped with the Tigray war, according to the US Department of Justice. Abraham Teklu Lemma, a Maryland resident who held a Top Secret security clearance, admitted on November 3, 2026, to conspiring to transmit US national defense information to the Ethiopian government. Prosecutors said the intelligence concerned an armed conflict in Ethiopia and was supplied to senior officials within the country’s political, military and intelligence institutions. In an official announcement , the Justice Department said Lemma worked as an information technology contractor at the National Reconnaissance Office, the US Department of State and the Department of Justice. According to court documents, Lemma collected and transmitted dozens of highly classified documents, notes, photographs and other materials between 2021 and his arrest in August 2023. Some of the information carried the Top Secret/Sensitive Compartmented Information classification, one of the highest levels of protection applied to US national security intelligence. Prosecutors said Lemma used his access as an IT administrator to retrieve classified information from government systems. He also copied sensitive information into handwritten notes and secretly carried them outside secure facilities. The Justice Department said these activities enabled him to pass restricted intelligence to Ethiopian government officials over an extended period. The case has drawn particular attention because the alleged espionage activities coincided with Ethiopia’s devastating northern conflict, which began in November 2020 and involved federal forces, TPLF-aligned forces and other armed actors. Although US authorities did not explicitly identify the conflict as the Tigray war in their November 3 announcement, the period covered by Lemma’s activities substantially overlaps with the fighting and its aftermath. The AFP report published on November 4 also noted the connection between the timeline of the intelligence disclosures and the conflict involving Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). US prosecutors said Lemma went beyond transmitting intelligence and, on some occasions, encouraged Ethiopian officials to take direct military action against armed groups opposing the federal government. In one exchange dated December 18, 2021, Lemma reportedly told an Ethiopian official that the opposing fighters had to be defeated to achieve peace. Later that day, according to the Justice Department, he transmitted additional information and wrote, “Please send Dro[nes].” The reference to drones is particularly significant because unmanned aircraft were used during Ethiopia’s northern conflict. However, the department did not identify a specific drone operation resulting from that communication or publicly establish that a particular attack was carried out because of Lemma’s message. US officials also said the intelligence he provided was used in military operations. Roman Rozhavsky, assistant director of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, stated that Ethiopian officials used classified national defense information supplied by Lemma during the conflict. Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg said Lemma had exploited his privileged access to remove sensitive information from secure facilities and transmit it to Ethiopian officials in the hope that it would help them target and kill opposing fighters. The department’s statements establish the US government’s account of the espionage and its military implications, but they do not publicly identify specific individuals killed, military targets attacked or operations directly attributable to the leaked information. Lemma’s guilty plea marks a major development in a case that began with his arrest in August 2023. He initially faced espionage-related charges after investigators accused him of unlawfully accessing and transferring classified US government information. Under the plea agreement announced on November 3, Lemma admitted to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government, an offense under US federal law. The agreement provides for a prison sentence ranging from 120 to 262 months, equivalent to 10 years to 21 years and 10 months, subject to acceptance by the court. US District Judge John D. Bates has scheduled sentencing for April 14, 2027, in Washington, D.C. The investigation was conducted by the FBI’s Washington Field Office, with prosecutors from the US Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia and the Justice Department’s National Security Division handling the case. The guilty plea also raises broader questions about the handling of classified American intelligence during Ethiopia’s conflict and the role of foreign intelligence information in military decision-making. For Ethiopia, the case brings renewed international attention to the 2020–2022 northern war and the relationship between Ethiopian government officials and individuals with access to sensitive US security information. The November 2022 Pretoria peace agreement formally ended major hostilities between Ethiopia’s federal government and the TPLF , although disputes over implementation and security arrangements have continued. The US authorities’ latest announcement does not identify the Ethiopian officials who received Lemma’s information or indicate whether any of them face criminal proceedings. Lemma remains awaiting sentencing, with the court expected to determine his punishment in April 2027. Continue Reading Ethiopia Ethiopian Opposition Alliance Calls for United Action Against Abiy Government Ethiopian opposition coalition renews its political demands and appeals for cooperation. Published 4 days ago on November 1, 2026 By Kulu Media News Desk A speaker reads a statement alongside two other men during an apparent Alliance for Survival press briefing. Photo credit: TMC/ Screenshot & Illustrated by Kulu Media The Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, a coalition of armed and political opposition groups, has issued a new statement calling for coordinated action against Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and outlining its position on Ethiopia’s political and security crises. In a four-page statement dated October 31, 2026, and shared on Facebook , the coalition, also known as the Alliance for Survival, accused the federal government of deepening the country’s political divisions, prolonging armed conflicts and failing to protect civilians. The alliance argued that Ethiopia’s current challenges require fundamental political change rather than measures undertaken by the existing administration. It presented cooperation among opposition organizations and communities as central to achieving that objective. The statement blamed the government for what the coalition described as widespread insecurity, displacement, human rights violations and deteriorating economic conditions. These allegations represent the alliance’s position and have not all been independently verified. The coalition also reiterated its opposition to the current federal administration and emphasized the need for a political arrangement that would protect the rights, security and participation of Ethiopia’s different communities. Its statement called for broader cooperation among political organizations, community representatives and other groups opposed to the government. It also addressed members of Ethiopia’s security institutions, urging them to reconsider their role in the country’s political and military conflicts. The alliance has previously identified the replacement of the current government and the establishment of an inclusive transitional administration as central objectives. The latest declaration continues that political position, although it does not establish that a transition has been agreed upon or that the coalition has secured additional territory or military support. The Alliance for Survival emerged in September 2026 as a coalition bringing together organizations with different political backgrounds and regional interests, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), the Amhara Fano National Movement and the Oromo Liberation Army. Its formation drew attention because some participating organizations have historically pursued competing political objectives or fought on opposing sides of earlier conflicts. Their cooperation reflects a shared opposition to the federal government, but does not necessarily mean that their wider political differences have been resolved. The new statement comes amid renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia, including confrontations involving TPLF-aligned forces, the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) and the Tigray Peace Force (TPF). Recent developments in Tigray have included the reported reentry of TPLF forces into Rama , followed by reports of drone strike damage in the area . The conflict has raised questions about the alliance’s military coordination and the extent to which its members can pursue a common strategy despite their differing political priorities. The declaration appears intended to reaffirm the coalition’s continued political cooperation and appeal for wider support. However, the statement does not independently establish a new joint military offensive, a formal agreement with additional organizations or a change in the balance of forces on the ground. No new response from the Ethiopian federal government to the October 31 statement had been independently verified at the time of writing. The alliance’s declaration adds to the political uncertainty surrounding Ethiopia’s continuing conflicts, although the practical implications of its latest calls remain unclear. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia has expelled six Sudanese diplomats amid escalating tensions between the two countries, particularly concerning allegations involving Sudan's paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia. The Ethiopian government ordered the diplomats, stationed at the Sudanese consulate in Assosa, to leave within 48 hours, although no specific reason was provided for the expulsion. This diplomatic rift comes as both nations accuse each other of involvement in armed conflicts affecting the Horn of Africa. Sudan has claimed that Ethiopia allows the RSF to launch drone attacks from its territory, while Ethiopia denies these allegations. The situation is further complicated by ongoing conflicts in Sudan and northern Ethiopia, raising concerns about regional stability. The expulsion of the Sudanese diplomats could hinder diplomatic engagement, and the broader implications of these tensions may affect security and relations in the region, particularly with neighboring countries like Eritrea and Egypt.

somalia.title: Somalia rejects Israeli ambassador to Somaliland and planned embassy in Hargeisa - Hiiraan Online
somalia.content: Somalia rejects Israeli ambassador to Somaliland and planned embassy in Hargeisa - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME POLITICS Somalia rejects Israeli ambassador to Somaliland and planned embassy in Hargeisa Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Wednesday November 4, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somalia rejected Israel’s accreditation of an ambassador to Somaliland and the laying of a cornerstone for a planned embassy in Hargeisa, calling the moves violations of its sovereignty and territorial integrity. The Foreign Ministry said Tuesday that the steps had been taken without the consent of Somalia’s federal government and declared them “null and void and without legal effect.” advertisements Israel’s first ambassador to Somaliland, Michael Lotem, presented his credentials to Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi Irro in Hargeisa last week, Israel’s Foreign Ministry announced Sunday. A cornerstone ceremony for a future Israeli embassy followed. “These actions, undertaken without the consent of the Federal Government of Somalia, constitute a flagrant violation of Somalia’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and unity,” Somalia’s Foreign Ministry said. Mogadishu maintains that Somaliland remains an integral part of Somalia and argues that it cannot independently establish diplomatic missions with foreign states. The ministry cited the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, arguing that the establishment of diplomatic relations and permanent missions requires the consent of the sovereign state. Somaliland declared independence from Somalia in 1991 and has governed itself for more than three decades with its own institutions, security forces and currency. Somalia rejects its claim to independence. Israel formally recognized Somaliland on Dec. 26, 2025, becoming the first U.N. member state to do so since Somaliland’s 1991 declaration. No other U.N. member state has followed. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar described the exchange of ambassadors as fulfillment of commitments made when the two sides established diplomatic relations and said Israel intended to deepen ties with Somaliland. Somaliland officials have welcomed the relationship and described the credential ceremony and planned embassy as milestones in expanding cooperation with Israel in areas including trade, security, technology and investment. Somalia, however, said Israel’s latest actions compounded what it described as the unlawful recognition of Somaliland. The African Union, Arab League, Organization of Islamic Cooperation and other regional bodies have previously rejected Israel’s recognition move and reaffirmed support for Somalia’s territorial integrity. “At a time of heightened insecurity in the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, actions that encourage fragmentation and disregard internationally recognised borders risk deepening tensions across an already fragile region,” Somalia’s Foreign Ministry said. Mogadishu demanded that Israel reverse the measures and called on governments and international organizations not to take steps that could confer legitimacy on them. The federal government also said it reserved the right to pursue diplomatic, political and legal measures under international law in defense of Somalia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. somalia.summary: Somalia has officially rejected Israel's appointment of an ambassador to Somaliland and the establishment of an embassy in Hargeisa, deeming these actions violations of its sovereignty and territorial integrity. The Somali Foreign Ministry stated that these developments occurred without the federal government's consent, rendering them "null and void." Israel's first ambassador to Somaliland, Michael Lotem, recently presented his credentials to Somaliland's President, followed by a cornerstone ceremony for the embassy. Somalia insists that Somaliland, which declared independence in 1991, remains an integral part of the nation and cannot independently engage in foreign diplomatic relations. The ministry cited the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations to support its stance. Somalia has called on Israel to reverse its actions and urged international bodies not to legitimize them. The African Union and other regional organizations have previously rejected Israel's recognition of Somaliland, emphasizing support for Somalia's territorial claims. Somalia reserves the right to pursue legal and diplomatic measures to defend its sovereignty. (158 words)

somalia.summary: The Ghana Football Association (GFA) has announced that media accreditation for the upcoming 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) qualifier between Ghana and Somalia is now open. Journalists and photographers wishing to cover the match at the Essipong Sports Stadium must submit their applications via email by 5:00 PM GMT on November 9, 2026. Each application must include a recent passport-sized photograph; those without will be disregarded. Successful applicants can collect their accreditation tags from designated locations based on their region. Due to limited space in the media tribune, specific allocations have been set for different media types: three for television, two for radio, and one for print/online portals. The total capacity for journalists at the stadium is 150, and a shortlist of accredited media will be published on November 9, 2026.

The building, funded by Direct Aid, will house the Genomics Laboratory, modern inpatient and outpatient facilities, and dedicated rooms for patient reception and medical consultations. The project is part of the hospital's expansion plan and is expected to enhance the country's capacity in specialized medical testing, research and the training of healthcare professionals. Related articles Benadir University Launches Ophthalmology Master's Program Somalia, UK Look to Bolster Disaster Preparedness as El Nino Looms The foundation stone was jointly laid by SIMAD University President Dr. Abdikarim Mohyiddin Ahmed, Direct Aid Director Mohamed Sheikh Bashir, and the Director General of the Ministry of Health and Social Care, Yusuf Hassan Isak. The hospital's expansion goes beyond infrastructure and medical equipment. It also includes plans to bring international doctors to Somalia to provide specialized healthcare services, potentially enabling Somali patients to access advanced medical care locally rather than travelling abroad. The ceremony comes as SIMAD University celebrates the 27th anniversary of its establishment, reflecting the university's continued efforts to advance education, research and healthcare services for the Somali community. Our Team Our Partners Contact Us Careers Facebook Twitter Instagram Youtube Spotify Linkedin Somalia Enters A New Era Of Self-Reliance Following UNTMIS Closure Gunnar Ivarsson November 4, 2026 No Comments A historic UN peacekeeping mission in Somalia has come to an end with the official closure of the United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) on October 31, 2026. The closure in Somalia is the culmination of a two-year transition which was initiated at the direct request of the Somali government. It brings to a close over thirty years of continuous UN political, state-building and peace missions. According to an official statement from the Spokesman for the UN Secretary-General, António Guterres, the drawdown of the mission is a significant milestone on the road to Somali sovereignty and self-reliance. Almost all government support is now being transferred to Somali institutions and resident UN development agencies. Under the surface of the diplomatic celebrations in Mogadishu, however, there becomes a real test: Can a federal government, so deeply divided along clan lines and still in the grip of an Al-Shabaab insurgency, manage to hold the institutions together without the benefit of an external referee? ​ The exit of UNTMIS is a significant development towards domestic ownership. For over 30 years, international peacekeepers and envoys have been essential as a bridge between the warring factions, helping rebuild the various ministries, monitoring human rights, and facilitating the sort of compromise that is so difficult to achieve in such a fractured political environment. The Somali authorities have long maintained that, as the country’s institutions mature, it is now time for Somalia to take full ownership of its internal political process. The handover of the institutions is still developing, however, and it is proceeding in the face of deep domestic division. The federal government’s determination to proceed with direct national elections has clearly alienated a number of regional administrations, and, as a result, the administrations in Puntland and Jubaland have both suspended their formal relationship with the federal capital. ​ An exit of a long-standing political mission may expose deep structural cracks within Somalia’s state-building project. An analysis by the International Crisis Group finds that UN political envoys have historically functioned as neutral buffers. They de-escalated political standoffs between Mogadishu and regional state leaders before they escalated into militarization. Without an impartial third-party presence in the capital, the risk of high-level conciliation spilling into localized armed confrontations increases. This distracts national forces from critical stabilization efforts. The ongoing reorganization of regional military forces compounds the security vacuum. The Star reports that the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) continues to support the forces in place, despite ongoing funding shortfalls. There are numerous diplomatic irritants among the various troop-contributing nations that have hampered efforts to coordinate a coherent defense. Al-Shabaab has repeatedly shown its capacity to leverage political infighting. When the political leadership in Mogadishu and the various regional capitals are engaged in constitutional brinkmanship, the troops on the ground are left without a strategy, and the local population is therefore exposed. ​ Securing a stable post-UNTMIS Somalia may require a re-think of the peacebuilding approach at the domestic level. The international community, led by the AU and IGAD, will need to support an immediate, institutionalized National Dialogue Conference. It will be critical for the federal and regional authorities to reach a consensus on the distribution of constitutional powers to ensure that they are properly represented in the governance structure. Just as important is the reallocation of resources towards community-level social cohesion. Sustainable security will depend on the consolidation of state authority in the liberated areas through community-based policing and the provision of public services. The international donor agencies that may remain in the country will need to be working directly with the local community elders and women’s peacebuilding networks, channeling the transition funding into local health, clean water, and climate adaptation projects to build resilience to the recurring droughts. Somalia’s path to lasting peace may well be defined by the extent to which its leaders are able to build democratic reconciliation. somalia.summary: The closure of the United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) on October 31, 2026, marks a pivotal moment in Somalia's journey toward self-reliance and sovereignty. This transition, initiated at the Somali government's request, ends over 30 years of UN involvement in peacekeeping and state-building efforts. While the UN's exit symbolizes a step towards domestic ownership, it also raises concerns about the stability of Somalia's federal government, which is currently grappling with internal divisions and the ongoing threat from Al-Shabaab. The absence of a neutral UN presence may exacerbate tensions between the federal government and regional administrations, particularly as Puntland and Jubaland have suspended ties with Mogadishu. Analysts suggest that a new approach to peacebuilding is essential, emphasizing the need for a National Dialogue Conference to address constitutional power distribution and promote community-level cohesion. The international community's support will be crucial in fostering sustainable security and resilience in the face of ongoing challenges.

Facebook Instagram X VKontakte Youtube Somali Guardian News Somalia Africa World Featured Editor Picks Editorials Home News Somalia Somalia’s president dismisses chief justice to forestall ruling on constitution Somalia’s president dismisses chief justice to forestall ruling on constitution November 4, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Somalia’s President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud on Wednesday dismissed Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf in a surprise move, days after the latter had taken up an opposition petition challenging the government’s new constitution and ordered the government to submit its defence. Mohamud appointed Ibrahim Eidle Suleiman, a member of the ruling party and a close associate of the president, as the new president of the Supreme Court, a move critics say undermines judicial independence. According to local media reports, Yusuf was on the verge of delivering a verdict on the opposition’s petition challenging the government’s new constitution, which parliament ratified earlier this year. The opposition and several regional states have denounced the process as unilateral and unconstitutional. Analysts say Mohamud moved pre-emptively to remove Yusuf before he could issue a potentially damaging ruling against the government, in what they described as a calculated move to forestall an adverse judicial decision. Weeks earlier, Bashe had issued a ruling ordering a rerun of the Galmudug regional elections, compelling the authorities to comply. This decision comes just days after Yusuf began addressing an opposition petition challenging the government's new constitution, which was ratified by parliament earlier this year. Ongoing conflict across the east continues to drive displacement and deepen humanitarian needs. Photo: UNOCHA/Wassy Kambale # Yemen Access constraints choke supplies, deepen hardship in Ta’iz The Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reports that almost 310,000 people in Yemen have now been forced to leave their homes since the beginning of August. Ta’iz city is running out of basic goods. Cargo transporters carrying flour and other staple foods on which Ta’iz markets depend have pulled their trucks back to the Al-Farsha area, where they sit stranded. Prices of essential items in Ta’iz city have risen by as much as fivefold. The collection of waste has also ground to a halt, with trucks prevented from reaching dumping sites. Piles of rubbish are building up across the city, increasing the risk of disease. UNICEF says it is alarmed that the Al-Suqyah Health Centre in Lahj governorate was attacked, resulting in the reported killing of 5 people, including health workers. The UNICEF-supported facility serves more than 1,700 people, including children. Humanitarian partners continue to reach people in need across Yemen. Since August, nearly 190,000 people have received food aid and nearly 140,000 have received emergency cash assistance. Partners working in health have now reached more than 9,000 displaced people through 60 mobile teams and health points and have supported 72 hospitals. The UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) say that nearly 5,400 newly displaced families have been registered for humanitarian cash assistance, and that 4,200 have received it. UNHCR has also provided cash for shelter to more than 2,100 families in the cities of Aden, Abyan and Lahj, and has 3,000 relief kits en route to Aden. Shelter remains a pressing need. Approximately 37,000 families are still awaiting shelter support, while 32,000 are awaiting basic household items. Since the escalation of hostilities in August, 28 displacement sites have opened or reopened, accommodating more than 20,000 people. The UN reiterates its call for the protection of civilians and for safe, sustained, and unimpeded humanitarian access, particularly to communities increasingly isolated by ongoing hostilities. Donations made to UN Crisis Relief help UN agencies and humanitarian NGOs reach people in Yemen with urgent support. # Occupied Palestinian Territory Gaza: Aid continues to reach families despite persistent insecurity OCHA reports that relief efforts in Gaza continue despite persistent insecurity. Yesterday, there was small arms fire near a UN-contracted facility in Deir al Balah and a convoy organized in Rafah. Thankfully, no injuries to UN staff or damage have been reported. Also yesterday, gunfire hit and damaged multiple tents in a displacement site in northern Rafah, reportedly causing injuries and forcing one of the humanitarian partners to leave the area, where it was working on flood control ahead of the rainy season. These incidents came amid continued reports on strikes hitting populated areas and causing civilian casualties across all areas of the Gaza Strip. Civilians – including humanitarian workers – must always be protected, and civilian objects – including humanitarian facilities and vehicles – must be spared. In the last week of October, the UN and its partners supported more than 70 households affected by incidents ranging from airstrikes to domestic fires, in which they lost shelters and other belongings. During that same week, partners leading on child protection reached nearly 4,500 boys and girls and more than 2,000 caregivers with mental health and psycho-social support. They identified almost 200 children who require individually tailored support, including 20 unaccompanied or separated children and 17 who are injured. Follow-up support continues for more than 2,000 children identified earlier as requiring such help. During the last week of October, partners provided vouchers to buy autumn clothes for more than 1,000 children without parental care. West Bank: Humanitarians support olive pickers amid violence, access restrictions Meanwhile in the West Bank, the olive harvest continues to be disrupted by Israeli settler violence and restrictions on Palestinian access to groves. Food security partners have provided harvesting tools and machinery across nearly 80 per cent of all identified hotspots, while partners leading on protection supported volunteer harvesting campaigns and protective presence. In most locations, however, assistance can reach only a limited number of olive pickers, due to funding shortfalls, violence and Israeli restrictions. # Democratic Republic of the Congo Dozens freed as violence disrupts aid, Ebola cases rise OCHA warns that violence continues to take a heavy toll on civilians across the eastern provinces in the Democratic Republic of the Congo , driving displacement, disrupting essential services and increasing humanitarian needs. In the province of Ituri, nearly 50 civilians were released yesterday in Mambasa territory after nearly three months in captivity. But the violence continues: according to local civil society organizations, at least 24 civilians were killed and 43 others abducted by armed groups in October alone. In the province of South Kivu, renewed fighting in Uvira territory since late October has forced 26 primary schools to shutter, depriving nearly 6,000 children of their educations. Meanwhile, in neighboring North Kivu province, clashes in Masisi and Lubero territories continue to force families from their homes and hamper humanitarian operations. The province also accounts for around 60 per cent of newly reported Ebola cases nationwide. As of 1 November, health authorities had reported more than 10,500 confirmed cases and over 5,100 deaths across the country. Insecurity continues to hinder work in several affected areas. Against this backdrop, an OCHA-coordinated inter-agency mission met with authorities in the territory of Beni territory in North Kivu, earlier this week to discuss humanitarian access, strengthen community engagement and support efforts to contain the outbreak. The UN reiterates its call on all parties to protect civilians, and ensure safe, sustained and unhindered humanitarian access. The fighting must not prevent humanitarians and health workers from reaching people who urgently need assistance. # Sudan Senior UN official warns drone attacks threaten life-saving care The Humanitarian Coordinator Denise Brown warns that stepped up drone strikes on civilian infrastructure are severely disrupting essential services and deepening civilian suffering across Sudan . Brown said that power stations and fuel facilities appear to be systematically targeted, causing widespread electricity outages, water supply disruptions and fuel shortages. Hospitals are directly impacted, including one outside Khartoum city where 25 patients had their life-saving dialysis treatment interrupted by a power outage. Hospitals are also struggling to provide maternity care and perform operations without electricity. Meanwhile, the UN Human Rights Office reports that drone strikes have intensified and spread across Sudan in the last two weeks, with at least 25 strikes on power and fuel infrastructure across 11 states. Yesterday, drone strikes reportedly hit energy infrastructure and residential neighbourhoods in the city of Ed Damazine in Blue Nile State, causing widespread power outages. Strikes also reportedly hit fuel stations in the states of River Nile and South Kordofan, causing civilian casualties and damaging vehicles. Insecurity also continues to force people from their homes. In South Kordofan, the International Organization for Migration reports that approximately 350 people were displaced from villages in the locality of Habila over the past two days. OCHA reiterates that civilians and civilian infrastructure must be protected. International humanitarian law prohibits attacks against civilians and objects indispensable to the survival of the civilian population. Despite the insecurity, the UN and its partners continue to deliver life-saving assistance. Last month, food assistance reached more than 20,000 people across the localities of Al Tina, Kornoi and Um Baru in North Darfur State. Nutrition and healthcare services also continued, while emergency water supplies reached more than 3,000 people in the localities of Kornoi and Um Baru. However, restricted access and funding shortages continue to hamper the humanitarian response. OCHA urgently calls for improved access and additional funding. With less than two months remaining in the year, Sudan's nearly $2.9 billion humanitarian response plan is just about 47 per cent funded , with $1.34 billion received so far. # Somalia Conflict, climate shocks push more Somalis into crisis OCHA reports that Somalia is facing a convergence of crises, including famine risk, conflict and insecurity, political tensions, El Niño-driven flooding, and drought. In South West State, the security situation has deteriorated significantly since late September, particularly in Baidoa and Buur Hakaba districts, uprooting civilians, including towards Baidoa town and towards the federal capital, Mogadishu. Humanitarian operations have also been disrupted where humanitarian needs are already severe. The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification identified a risk of famine in the town of Buur Hakaba earlier this year, but this was averted through a concerted humanitarian response in the area. But the latest IPC analysis, published in September, warns that famine now threatens displaced communities in the town of Baidoa. Despite the challenges, the UN and its humanitarian partners provided 1.7 million people with at least one form of humanitarian aid across Somalia. Somalia also remains on the front line of the climate crisis, with El Nino compounding the risks as the peak of the Deyr rainy season approaches, while parts of the north of the country continue to suffer from drought. Heavy rains have already triggered flash floods in several areas, affecting thousands of people. The authorities and humanitarian partners are tracking rising river levels across multiple states. In areas at greatest risk, partners have positioned emergency supplies and boats in advance and have begun distributing cash assistance to families. Last month, Emergency Relief Coordinator, Tom Fletcher, approved an allocation of US$16 million for Somalia from the UN Central Emergency Response Fund, alongside 11 other underfunded crises. But funding remains critically short. Somalia's $852 million humanitarian response plan for this year is only one-third funded, even as needs continue to grow. somalia.summary: The Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) highlights critical humanitarian crises in Yemen, the Occupied Palestinian Territory, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Sudan, and Somalia. In Yemen, ongoing conflict has displaced nearly 310,000 people since August, with Ta’iz city facing severe shortages of essential goods and rising prices. In Gaza, aid efforts continue amid persistent violence, while the West Bank sees disruptions in olive harvesting due to Israeli settler violence. The Democratic Republic of the Congo faces escalating violence, with significant civilian casualties and a rising Ebola outbreak. In Sudan, drone strikes on civilian infrastructure are exacerbating humanitarian needs, disrupting essential services like healthcare. Meanwhile, Somalia grapples with a convergence of crises, including famine risks and climate shocks, affecting over 1.7 million people. OCHA emphasizes the urgent need for humanitarian access and funding to address these escalating crises and protect civilians in affected regions.

somalia.summary: The Federal Government of Somalia has relieved two officials from their positions, effective November 4, 2026. The dismissed officials are Mr. Said Mohamed Mahmoud, who served as the State Minister at the Ministry of Public Works, Reconstruction and Housing, and Ms. Fartun Abdikadir Farah, the Deputy Minister at the Ministry of Ports and Marine Transport. The announcement was made by the Somali National News Agency (SONNA), although specific reasons for their dismissal were not disclosed. This decision comes amid ongoing developments in the Somali government, including recent meetings on regional trade agreements and security discussions in the Gulf of Aden. The changes in leadership reflect the government's efforts to address various national issues and enhance its administrative effectiveness. The situation remains dynamic as the government continues to navigate challenges in governance and public service.

football.summary: أعلن الاتحاد الإفريقي لكرة القدم (الكاف) عن تفاصيل حفل جوائز الأفضل في إفريقيا لعام 2026، المقرر إقامته في 7 ديسمبر في لاجوس، نيجيريا. تم ترشيح فريق الهلال السوداني لجائزة أفضل نادي في إفريقيا، بالإضافة إلى ترشيح لاعب الهلال عبد الرزاق عبد الرؤوف لجائزة أفضل لاعب. تشمل قائمة الأندية المرشحة أيضًا الزمالك المصري، الترجي الرياضي التونسي، صنداونز الجنوب إفريقي، والعديد من الأندية المغربية والجزائرية. يأتي هذا الترشيح في ظل الأداء المتميز للهلال في البطولات الإفريقية، مما يعكس تطور الفريق على الساحة القارية. يُعتبر هذا الإنجاز خطوة مهمة في تاريخ النادي، ويعزز من مكانته بين الأندية الكبرى في إفريقيا. يتطلع الهلال وجماهيره إلى تحقيق المزيد من النجاحات في المستقبل القريب.

اتصل بنا تاق برس - اخبار السودان والعالم الرئيسية أخبار عاجلة سياسية منوعات وثقافة إقتصاد رياضة علوم وتكنلوجيا مقالات أخري تقارير صحة الرئيسية أخبار رياضة الهلال السوداني يواجه رايون سبورت بالقوة الضاربة.. وزينباور يرفض المغامرة بالبدلاء الهلال السوداني يواجه رايون سبورت بالقوة الضاربة.. وزينباور يرفض المغامرة بالبدلاء بواسطة editor في نوفمبر 3, 2026 215 مشاركة متابعات تاق برس – يستعد الهلال السوداني لخوض مواجهة مهمة أمام رايون سبورت الرواندي، غداً الأربعاء، ضمن منافسات الجولة الثامنة من الدوري الرواندي الممتاز، في مباراة يتطلع خلالها الفريق إلى مواصلة انتصاراته وتعزيز موقعه في جدول الترتيب. ويتجه المدير الفني للهلال، الألماني جوزيف زينباور، بحسب صحيفة آكشن سبورت، إلى الاعتماد على عناصره الأساسية، رافضاً تكرار تجربة الدفع بتشكيلة يغلب عليها البدلاء، التي كلفت الفريق خسارة ثقيلة أمام مارين بثلاثة أهداف دون مقابل. ويستعيد زينباور موقعه في المنطقة الفنية بعد انتهاء عقوبة إيقافه لمباراة واحدة، وسط اتجاه للاعتماد على عدد من العناصر الأساسية، من بينهم مصطفى كرشوم وياسر عوض وأرنست لوزولو، مع التركيز على تعزيز الانضباط التكتيكي والتنظيم الدفاعي. وتكتسب المواجهة أهمية إضافية باعتبارها اختباراً مهماً للهلال قبل انطلاق مشواره في دور المجموعات لدوري أبطال أفريقيا، حيث يواجه حوريا كوناكري الغيني يوم 28 نوفمبر الجاري. وتُقام المباراة على ملعب كيغالي بيليه عند السادسة والنصف مساءً، وكان الهلال قد استأنف تدريباته بالعاصمة الرواندية كيغالي، وسط أجواء من الحماس والتركيز، استعداداً للمواجهة المرتقبة. الدوري الرواندي الممتاز الهلال السوداني كرة القدم 215 مشاركة أخبار ذات صلة رياضة الهلال السوداني في مجموعة نارية.. تعرف على منافسيه في دوري أبطال إفريقيا رياضة الهلال السوداني يقترب football.content: المريخ يربك تحضيرات الهلال لمجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا المريخ يربك تحضيرات الهلال لمجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا مباريات اليوم رياضات كرة القدم الأخبار فيديو البطولات البرامج دول المريخ يربك تحضيرات الهلال لمجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا من ديربي السودان الكبير بين الغريمين الهلال والمريخ (winwin) 3 نوفمبر 2026 المريخ يربك تحضيرات الهلال لمجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا الهلال السوداني المريخ دوري أبطال أفريقيا الدوري السوداني الممتاز كرة قدم حافظ محمد أحمد الخرطوم winwin أضفنا الى 'غوغل' عاد نجم نادي الهلال والمنتخب السوداني، مصطفى كرشوم، إلى الواجهة بقوة، مقدمًا مستويات مميزة في الآونة الأخيرة، إذ استعاد بريقه الكامل خلال مباراتي "صقور الجديان" في التصفيات الأفريقية، ومباريات فريقه في الدورين التمهيديين لمسابقة دوري أبطال أفريقيا . وقد أشعل المدافع المتألق سباقًا مبكرًا بين قطبي الكرة السودانية مع اقتراب دخوله "الفترة الحرة"، إذ يسعى النادي الأحمر لاستعادة نجمه السابق، بينما يتمسك "الأزرق" بجوهرته بعد أن وجد ضالته في المدافع الفذ، الذي يصنفه الخبراء بأنه أفضل لاعب في البلاد خلال السنوات الأخيرة. الهلال يتحرك للحفاظ على نجمه في هذا السياق، كشفت مصادر موثوقة لموقع "winwin" أن إدارة نادي الهلال استشعرت الخطر، وبدأت تحركاتها مبكرًا لتأمين بقاء نجمها وتمديد تعاقده قبل دخوله الفترة الحرة؛ وذلك بعد أن نجح اللاعب في إعادة الصلابة والهيبة لدفاع الفريق، الذي عانى من تذبذب واضح في مستوياته السابقة. ويعد كرشوم ظاهرة نادرة في الملاعب السودانية؛ نظرًا لسلوكه الاحترافي وانضباطه العالي، فضلًا عن ثبات مستواه وقلة أخطائه. وفي هذا الصدد، فتحت إدارة النادي برئاسة هشام السوباط باب التفاوض مع اللاعب؛ لضمان استمراره في صفوف الفريق لمدة عامين إضافيين على الأقل. اقرأ أيضًا اكتسح الترشيحات.. نجم الهلال السوداني يقترب من تتويج خاص خاص | نجم السودان يفتح النار ويشرح أسباب خيبة المريخ قاريًا وكشفت مصادر عالية الثقة، أنّ إدارة المريخ تعتزم استعادة نجمها، استجابة للمطالبات الجماهيرية الملحة، ونظرًا لقيمته الفنية العالية؛ إذ تعد عودته مكسبًا مضاعفًا باعتباره أفضل مدافع في البلاد، وسيشكل إضافة نوعية للفريق. كما يخدم هذا التوجه خطط إدارة الرئيس مجاهد سهل في التحضير للجمعية العمومية المقررة في مارس 2027 لانتخاب مجلس إدارة جديد، حيث ستحظى الإدارة بدعم كبير إذا نجحت في استعادة كرشوم الذي قدم سنوات مميزة مع الفريق، وأسهم بفاعلية في بلوغه دور المجموعات بدوري أبطال أفريقيا 3 نسخ متتالية. وقد أثارت هذه الرغبة قلق الغريم التقليدي الهلال الذي يستعد بقوة لمرحلة المجموعات. ومن المتوقع أن يحسم اللاعب مستقبله خلال الفترة المقبلة؛ ففي حال تمديد عقده مع ناديه الحالي، ستتلاشى آمال عودته للمريخ مستقبلًا، لا سيما مع بلوغه سن الـ35 عامًا، واقترابه من الاعتزال، أما في حال تعثر مفاوضات التجديد مع الهلال فسيمنح ذلك المريخ الضوء الأخضر لضمه. النشرة البريدية اشترك معنا بالنشرة البريدية football.summary: تسبب نادي المريخ في إرباك تحضيرات نادي الهلال السوداني لمجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا، حيث عاد المدافع مصطفى كرشوم إلى الواجهة بعد تقديمه مستويات مميزة مع منتخب بلاده وناديه. يسعى الهلال للحفاظ على كرشوم، الذي يعتبر من أفضل اللاعبين في السودان، من خلال التفاوض لتمديد عقده قبل دخوله الفترة الحرة. في المقابل، يخطط المريخ لاستعادة نجمه السابق، استجابة لمطالب الجماهير، مما يزيد من حدة المنافسة بين الناديين. كرشوم، الذي ساهم بشكل كبير في نجاح الهلال في السنوات الأخيرة، قد يحسم مستقبله قريبًا. إذا نجح الهلال في تجديد عقده، ستتلاشى آمال المريخ في ضمه، خاصة مع اقتراب اللاعب من الاعتزال. بينما إذا تعثرت المفاوضات، قد يفتح ذلك المجال أمام المريخ لاستعادة خدماته، مما يزيد من التوتر بين الغريمين التقليديين في كرة القدم السودانية.

football.summary: تواجه الهلال السوداني فريق بيراميدز في مباراة ضمن دوري أبطال إفريقيا، حيث انتهت المباراة بالتعادل السلبي 0-0. أقيمت المباراة في 8 يناير 2027، وهي جزء من مرحلة المجموعات للموسم 2026/2027. يتواجد الهلال السوداني في المجموعة A، التي تضم أيضًا الترجي الرياضي التونسي وبيترو أتلتيكو ونواذيبو. على الرغم من عدم تسجيل أي أهداف، إلا أن المباراة كانت مثيرة، حيث حاول كلا الفريقين السيطرة على مجريات اللعب. الهلال السوداني يسعى لاستعادة توازنه بعد سلسلة من النتائج المتباينة في الدوري الرواندي، بينما بيراميدز يأمل في تحسين أدائه في البطولة. تتواصل المنافسات في دوري أبطال إفريقيا، حيث يتطلع كل فريق لتحقيق نتائج إيجابية في المباريات القادمة لتعزيز فرصه في التأهل إلى الأدوار المتقدمة.

football.title: اكتسح الترشيحات.. نجم الهلال السوداني يقترب من تتويج خاص - winwin
football.content: اكتسح الترشيحات.. نجم الهلال السوداني يقترب من تتويج خاص اكتسح الترشيحات.. نجم الهلال السوداني يقترب من تتويج خاص مباريات اليوم رياضات كرة القدم الأخبار فيديو البطولات البرامج دول اكتسح الترشيحات.. نجم الهلال السوداني يقترب من تتويج خاص لاعبو الهلال السوداني (Facebook/ Al Hilal S.C) 2 نوفمبر 2026 اكتسح الترشيحات.. نجم الهلال السوداني يقترب من تتويج خاص الهلال السوداني الدوري السوداني الممتاز كرة قدم حافظ محمد أحمد الخرطوم winwin أضفنا الى 'غوغل' أشعلت جماهير الهلال السوداني منافسة خاصة بين نجوم الفريق، مصطفى كرشوم وأرنست لوزولو وياسر عوض، للفوز بجائزة "أفضل لاعب في شهر أكتوبر" التي خصصتها إدارة النادي لتحفيز اللاعبين ورفع مستوى أدائهم. ويعد المدافع مصطفى كرشوم المرشح الأبرز لنيل الجائزة بفضل مستواه المتميز الذي قدمه خلال الشهر الماضي، لا سيما في مباراتي سيداما بونا الإثيوبي بالدور التمهيدي الثاني لمسابقة دوري أبطال أفريقيا، مما جعله يحظى باهتمام واسع من الجماهير، وتقدم اللاعب بوضوح مكتسحًا زميليه مقتربًا من تحقيق مكسب مهم قبل صدامات قارية مرتقبة. في المقابل، يواصل ياسر عوض حضوره القوي في المنافسة للشهر الثاني على التوالي، بعد أن كان مرشحًا بارزًا في شهر سبتمبر/ أيلول الماضي. ونجح اللاعب المحلي في قلب الطاولة على المحترف الكونغولي ستيفن إيبويلا وأزاحه عن مركز الظهير الأيمن، ليستأثر بفرصة المشاركة بصفة أساسية بعد أن كسب ثقة المدرب جوزيف زينباور. اقرأ أيضًا بعد رسائل الحزم.. مدرب الهلال يتلقى دعما قبل مواعيد حاسمة الهلال السوداني يستعيد توازنه بفوز ثمين في الدوري الرواندي بدوره، فرض أرنست لوزولو نفسه ضمن قائمة المرشحين بعد أن نجح في تسجيل هدف رائع في شباك سيداما بونا الإثيوبي، مقدمًا مستويات باهرة، ومسهمًا في تحقيق فريقه لانتصارات محلية وقارية. كرشوم يواصل تألقه مع الهلال السوداني من جانبه، يمثل مدافع الهلال السوداني مصطفى كرشوم ظاهرة نادرة في الملاعب السودانية، لاستمرار تألقه ومحافظته على مستواه مع المنتخب وفريقه، مما جعله ضمن قائمة أفضل اللاعبين في البلاد خلال السنوات الأخيرة. ورغم بلوغه سن الـ35، يتطلع اللاعب لظهورٍ لافت في الموسم الحالي، خاصة مع اقتراب دخوله الفترة الحرة، طامحًا في الحصول على تقييم يتناسب مع موهبته وخبراته، واغتنام فرصة التجديد الأخيرة قبل اعتزاله. من المتوقع أن تعلن إدارة النادي عن الفائز بالجائزة في حفلٍ مصغر دأبت على إقامته دوريًا. مع العلم أنّ المحترف الموريتاني في صفوف الفريق، أحمد سالم مبارك، كان قد توج بالجائزة عن شهر سبتمبر/ أيول الماضي وسط حفاوة كبيرة من زملائه، فيما يعد مصطفى كرشوم المرشح الأوفر حظا لنيل الجائزة عن شهر أكتوبر. النشرة البريدية اشترك معنا بالنشرة البريدية لتصلك آخر أخبار الرياضة اشترك معنا دول كرة القدم الأخبار الدوريات الفرق رياضات التنس كرة السلة رياضات ميكانيكية مبارايات اليوم الأخبار البرامج الفيديو عن الموقع تواصل معنا أعلن معنا وظائف سياسة الخصوصية الشروط والأحكام football.summary: يقترب نجم الهلال السوداني، المدافع مصطفى كرشوم، من الفوز بجائزة "أفضل لاعب في شهر أكتوبر" التي أطلقتها إدارة النادي لتحفيز اللاعبين. وقد أظهر كرشوم أداءً متميزًا خلال الشهر الماضي، خاصة في مباراتي فريقه ضد سيداما بونا الإثيوبي في دوري أبطال أفريقيا، مما جعله المرشح الأبرز لنيل الجائزة. ينافسه في هذه الجائزة كل من ياسر عوض، الذي قدم أداءً قويًا للشهر الثاني على التوالي، وأرنست لوزولو، الذي سجل هدفًا رائعًا في نفس البطولة. يُعتبر كرشوم، الذي يبلغ من العمر 35 عامًا، من أبرز اللاعبين في السودان، ويأمل في تحقيق تقييم يتناسب مع خبراته قبل اعتزاله. من المتوقع أن تُعلن إدارة النادي عن الفائز في حفل مصغر، حيث كان أحمد سالم مبارك قد فاز بالجائزة عن شهر سبتمبر.
